summary:
Feed conversion ratio is the kilograms of feed it takes to add one kilogram of gain. It returns total liveweight gain, feed conversion ratio, feed efficiency (gain per kg feed) and feed cost per kg of gain, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator returns FCR, its inverse (feed efficiency), the feed cost per kilogram of gain and the improvement from a target FCR. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Feed Conversion Ratio
sections.html:
FCR = feed consumed ÷ liveweight gain; feed efficiency = gain ÷ feed = 1 ÷ FCR

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
feeddry or as-fed feed consumedkg
gainweight gained over the same periodkg
FCRfeed conversion ratiokg/kg

Where the relationship comes from. Feed conversion ratio is the standard performance measure in livestock recording schemes; values quoted here follow typical commercial breed benchmarks.

sections.title: How do I use the Feed Conversion Ratio?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: feed offered of 1,200 kg, starting weight of 30 kg, finishing weight of 105 kg, animals lost of 0 head, feed price of 0.42 per kg, target fcr of 2.6.

Substituting them into the formula gives total liveweight gain of 75 kg, feed conversion ratio of 16 kg/kg, feed efficiency (gain per kg feed) of 0.0625 kg/kg, feed cost per kg of gain of 6.72 per kg, feed per surviving animal of 1,200 kg, feed the target fcr would need of 195 kg.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
below 1.8Excellentmodern broilers and well-run pig units
1.8 – 2.5Goodtypical efficient pig finishing
2.5 – 4.0Averagebeef feedlot, older genetics
above 4.0Poorcheck feed wastage, health and weighing accuracy

  • Always compare FCR over the same weight range. A pig from 30 to 105 kg converts far better than the same pig from 8 to 30 kg, because maintenance is spread over more gain.

  • Feed efficiency is the same information upside down: an FCR of 2.5 is an efficiency of 0.40 kg of gain per kg of feed.

  • Deaths do not change FCR as calculated on surviving animals unless you divide by the weight gain of the animals actually placed, which is what makes the figure honest.

  • Report whether the feed weight is as-fed or dry matter. Silage at 35% dry matter looks like a wonderful FCR until you realise most of the weight was water.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Recording feed delivered to the bunk instead of feed consumed — spillage and refusals inflate the number.
  • Weighing animals once, at the end, after a different interval for each pen.
  • Comparing FCR across species: poultry, pigs and cattle live on completely different scales.

faq.q: What is a good feed conversion ratio for broilers?
faq.a: Around 1.5–1.7 kg of feed per kg of liveweight for modern broiler strains over a 42-day cycle.

faq.q: Why does my FCR get worse as animals get heavier?
faq.a: Maintenance requirements scale with body weight while gain does not, so the marginal cost of each extra kilogram rises.

faq.q: Does adding water to feed change FCR?
faq.a: It changes as-fed FCR but not dry-matter FCR, which is why dry-matter figures are the only ones that compare across farms.

faq.q: What does the Feed Conversion Ratio actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns total liveweight gain, feed conversion ratio, feed efficiency (gain per kg feed) and feed cost per kg of gain. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
